title: Review alate's privacy policy for content that doesn't belong in a privacy policy
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: Tessellate-Studio/tessellate-pages. Labels: help wanted, P0. Owner request 2026-09-18: double-check `alate/privacy-policy.html` (v5 after #12) for anything that typically should **not** be in a privacy policy, and for anything legally required that is missing or weak. This is a review task: list findings with a recommendation each, and change nothing without an owner decision.

## Candidates already spotted (2026-09-18, while checking #12)
These are observations for the reviewer to confirm or dismiss. None of them is a legal opinion.

1. **§14: "Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance."** This is a terms-of-service clause. A privacy policy informs; it doesn't collect agreement, and under GDPR consent can't be inferred from continued use. The usual wording is "we will notify you of material changes" (in-app or by email) instead.
2. **§11 Grievance Officer shows a personal first name ("Saptami").** DPDP needs a reachable contact. Whether to publish a person's name or a role plus `privacy@` is an owner choice. Flagged because it puts a real person's name on a public page.
3. **Implementation detail: "AsyncStorage" (§7 Security).** It's internal tech jargon that means nothing to a reader. "Stored in the app's private storage on your device" says the same thing.
4. **Changelog-style history in the body:** "Crash reports previously carried an approximate country… as of September 2026 we strip that" (§1f). History usually lives in a change log, not in the current statement of practice.
5. **Age thresholds: 16+ age gate vs. under-18 parental consent for India (§11/§12).** The two sections are internally consistent, but the app only gates at 16. Confirm the India wording matches what the app actually does, so it doesn't promise a check the app doesn't run.

**Package:** `gdpr.compliance`
**Standard:** GDPR

This policy uses **boolean rules**: `default <name> := false` with a matching
`<name> if { ... }`. There are roughly **21** of them.

For each, write a case with input that makes it true, and one where it stays
false. Boolean rules are where the `{}` trap bites — a rule with no `default`

report object.

### Done when

- [ ] `opa test frameworks/privacy/gdpr -v` passes
- [ ] Each rule has a case that exercises it
- [ ] At least one case asserts nothing fires on compliant input
- [ ] The compliance report is asserted to be a **populated object on empty input**, not `{}`

### Where to put it

`frameworks/privacy/gdpr/tests/test_gdpr_compliance.rego`, package `gdpr.compliance_test`.

The pattern to copy, and the `array.concat` trap, are in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). The full queue of untested
policies is in [COVERAGE.md](../blob/main/COVERAGE.md).

description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: aws-samples/sample-aiml-security-assessment. Labels: enhancement, help wanted. ## Summary

Security practitioners and compliance teams need to map findings to established AI governance frameworks. This issue tracks adding **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)** and **ISO/IEC 42001** control mappings so findings can be traced to those frameworks in the report.

## Approach — OWASP-style compliance standards

Add each framework as a first-class compliance standard following the existing **OWASP Top 10 for LLM** pattern, not new per-check fields. OWASP is derived by *mapping existing BR/SM/AC/FS checks* into a dedicated prefixed section (`OW-`) registered in `COMPLIANCE_STANDARDS` (`generate_consolidated_report/report_template.py`), which already carries an explicit `# Future: {"slug": "nist", "name": "NIST AI RMF", "prefix": "NR-", ...}` placeholder. NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 are the same shape: mapping-based derivation from existing checks into their own standard sections.

Each standard is added via the documented **seven-site wire-up** in `docs/DEVELOPER_GUIDE.md` → "Adding a Compliance Standard (OWASP-style)", mirroring `owasp_assessments/app.py` (`OWASP_CHECK_MAPPINGS`, `get_owasp_reference_url`) and its `COMPLIANCE_STANDARDS` registry entry.

- Mapping values are **lists** — one source check may emit multiple framework rows.
- Every mapped source `Check_ID` must still exist in its scanner; every emitted framework ID must be documented in the catalog docs.
- An `N/A` source row produces `Severity=Informational` on the mapped row (never inherits High/Medium).

> **Note:** ISO/IEC 42001 is not yet in the `COMPLIANCE_STANDARDS` future placeholders (NIST AI RMF and EU AI Act are). It gets a new standard slug/prefix, wired the same way.

title: AI Act: security and robustness guidance for high-risk systems
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: mdiamantino/awesome-eu-cybersec. Labels: help wanted, coverage gap. Article 15 requires accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity for high-risk AI systems. The standardisation work at CEN-CENELEC JTC 21, the AI Office guidance and national regulator material are all in scope. Generic AI-safety content with no EU legal hook is not.

### What is wanted

Entries in `data/resources/governance-risk-policy.yml`. One good entry is a complete
contribution; there is no need to fill the whole gap.

### How to do it

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mdiamantino/awesome-eu-cybersec && cd awesome-eu-cybersec
make install
$EDITOR data/resources/governance-risk-policy.yml
make build     # regenerates README.md and the exports
make check     # the same thing CI runs
```

Commit the YAML change together with the regenerated `README.md`,
`data/ecosystem.yml` and `data/ecosystem.json`, then open the pull request.

### Entry format

```yaml
- name: Vulnerability-Lookup
  url: https://github.com/vulnerability-lookup/vulnerability-lookup
  description: Software from CIRCL Luxembourg that correlates advisories from national
    vulnerability databases and CSAF providers and supports coordinated disclosure workflows.
  subcategory: Vulnerability Intelligence
  tags: [cvd, correlation, circl]
  entry_type: Tool
  country_or_body: Luxembourg/CIRCL
  hosting_note: '[Open Source]'
  license: AGPL-3.0-or-later
  confidence: high
  last_verified: '2026-09-16'
```

Field reference and the scope rules are in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/mdiamantino/awesome-eu-cybersec/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

### The one bar

Open the URL yourself and confirm the page is what you say it is. An entry you
have not read does not go in, and `confidence: high` means you fetched it.
Quote what you saw in the pull request.

Not sure whether something qualifies? Ask in this issue before writing the entry.
That is what it is for.

title: docs: EU AI Act high-risk date in COMPETITIVE-ANALYSIS.md was superseded before it arrived
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: arthurpanhku/dvalincode. Labels: documentation, good first issue. ## What

`docs/COMPETITIVE-ANALYSIS.md` cites **「EU AI Act 高风险义务 2026-08-02 生效」** as regulatory tailwind in three places — lines 88, 136 and 270.

That date no longer holds. **Regulation (EU) 2026/1744** (the Digital Omnibus on AI) was published in the Official Journal on **24 July 2026** and entered into force on **27 July 2026**. It defers:

- Annex III standalone high-risk systems: 2 August 2026 → **2 December 2027**
- Annex I high-risk in regulated products: → **2 August 2028**

The Commission's stated reason was that neither industry nor CEN/CENELEC would have harmonised standards ready, and the conformity-assessment infrastructure the Act assumes had not matured.

## Why it's worth fixing rather than leaving

The document argues Dvalin's hash-chain audit and Evidence Pack catch a regulatory wave. That argument survives — but a security reviewer who follows this file will notice the date passed with nothing happening, which undercuts the surrounding claims more than the correction costs.

**The tailwind is rescheduled, not cancelled**, and the doc can say so more precisely than it does now:

- **Article 50 transparency obligations have applied since the start of September 2026** — that is live today.
- Two new prohibitions land in December 2026.
- The quality-management standard to build against already exists.

So the honest framing is nearer-term in one respect and much later in another, rather than simply "delayed."

## Acceptance

- The three citations state the current dates and their legal source (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744).
- The distinction between deferred high-risk obligations and the Article 50 obligations already in force is explicit.

Sources: [Gibson Dunn](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement-postponed-high-risk-deadlines-and-other-key-changes/) · [CSA — Deferred, Not Cancelled](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.or …

title: Add industry file: Legal Tech
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: glacierphonk/naming. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, good first issue, industry. ## Task

Add a legal tech naming guide at \`industries/legaltech.md\`. Depends on #180.

## Why legal tech naming is distinct

- **Authority and gravitas required** — lawyers are conservative buyers. Playful names feel unserious
- **Latin legal vocabulary** — massive untapped naming source (habeas, certiorari, amicus, pro bono — but also pretentious if misused)
- **Trust + precision** — legal products handle sensitive documents, contracts, privileged communications
- **Regulated profession** — \"attorney\" and \"lawyer\" have legal meaning. Names that imply legal advice when the product doesn't provide it are risky
- **Old industry meets new tech** — naming must bridge tradition and innovation

## Sections to cover

- Case studies: Harvey (AI), Clio, Ironclad, Everlaw, LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer
- Anti-patterns: \"Legal[X]\", \"[X]Law\", fake Latin, over-gravitas
- Territory map: Shield/protection, compass/guidance, ledger/record, bridge/arbitration

## Before submitting

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and run \`markdownlint-cli2 '**/*.md'\` before pushing.

title: [Feature]: Add evidence-gated shadow evaluation for consequential policy decisions
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: rlaope/oh-my-hermes. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, area/routing, area/workflows, area/quality, risk/contract-change, needs-triage, priority/P1, impact/high. ## Problem

OMH makes several consequential policy decisions through deterministic rules and static fixtures: route selection, coding-owner recommendation, task-scale routing, continuation state, context-budget actions, and verification tiering. Those rules can be changed and regression-tested, but current `main` has no shared way to run a candidate decision policy in shadow mode beside the active policy, retain bounded disagreement evidence, and require reviewed evidence before promotion.

Without that lifecycle, maintainers can prove that a proposed rule passes known fixtures but cannot answer whether it disagrees on real eligible decisions, whether those disagreements cluster around one input class, or whether latency, failure, and coverage make the candidate safe to activate. Each subsystem must either invent its own comparison log or promote directly from test evidence.

## Complete user goal

As an OMH maintainer, I want any consequential deterministic decision point to register an active policy and an optional candidate policy, compare them without changing live behavior, aggregate privacy-safe and revision-bound evidence, and permit activation only through an explicit reviewed promotion decision. The workflow must remain useful with local deterministic candidates and caller-supplied evaluator receipts; OMH core must not require a hosted model or provider call.

## Intended surfaces

- Hermes chat or wrapper
- Hermes runtime or handoff
- All executors (executor-neutral)
